mainText:
A homicide investigation in Rotorua after three people died at a house in Glenholme leads this morning, alongside a fresh flu surge straining children's hospitals nationwide.

New Zealand.

Police have confirmed a homicide investigation after three people died overnight at a house on High Street in Glenholme, Rotorua. This follows yesterday's initial report of the deaths. No further detail has been released. Investigations continue.

Flu season is hitting children's hospitals hard. About seventy children with the most severe respiratory symptoms have been admitted each week for the past month to Auckland's Kidz First and Starship hospitals. Extra paediatricians have been called in. Paediatrician Dame Teuila Percival wants free flu vaccines for all children next winter.

Tauranga Hospital Emergency Department nurses have declared a state of emergency, saying exceptional demand has become their daily reality. This follows similar declarations by ED staff at other hospitals nationwide. It adds pressure on Te Whatu Ora, which has faced repeated criticism this year over emergency department conditions.

The Reserve Bank's October the twenty eighth OCR review is back in play as a live pre-election question, after average ninety one octane petrol prices topped three dollars ten a litre. Global oil prices surged above one hundred US dollars a barrel after renewed Iran and United States fighting. The election falls just over a week later, on November the seventh.

New Zealand's housing market has slowed sharply. Just five thousand four hundred and thirty homes changed hands in August, the sixth lowest August tally in thirty five years. Auckland's median time to sell reached fifty four days against a ten year average of forty three. Wellington reached sixty days against an average of forty one.

A car hit a pedestrian on Ferry Road in Woolston, Christchurch, early this morning. Two people were injured, one critically. The road remains blocked and the Serious Crash Unit is investigating.

World.

Yemen's Houthi forces continue to threaten Red Sea shipping despite earlier pledges to stop targeting vessels. The world's top three container operators say they remain wary of the routes. United States Vice President J.D. Vance says the administration is on top of the Houthi advance. This follows Monday's reported seizure of the Bab al Mandeb strait.

Rwanda backed rebels have entered Goma, a designated safe haven city in eastern Congo. Residents reported gunfire and shelling as Congolese troops were overrun. United Nations officials estimate more than one million displaced people are now inside the city. Aid access is a growing concern.

Palestinians have begun streaming back on foot into northern Gaza after Israel allowed civilians to cross a military zone bisecting the enclave, following a deadlock over hostage releases. Hamas has released four female Israeli soldiers under the ceasefire deal, the second such release since the multiphase agreement took effect. Ninety one hostages remain in Israeli custody according to Israeli officials.

A ferry capsized in the Java Sea off Indonesia. Six people are dead and one hundred and thirty remain missing from the Virgo Transport eight. Ships and helicopters continue searching. It follows the Vanuatu ferry disaster, where more than thirty people remain missing after the MV Matui sank in rough seas, exposing what an inquiry has called a gap between warnings and action.

Technology.

Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark says artificial intelligence kill switches, mechanisms allowing labs to shut down a model, may need to become mandatory. He says most labs currently have different informal approaches. The United Kingdom government has rejected the idea, with the Cabinet Office saying it cannot simply turn AI off. It follows chief executive Dario Amodei's renewed call this week for AI development to slow down, and a former Anthropic researcher telling the BBC staff are genuinely frightened for humanity's future. United States President Donald Trump has dismissed the warnings as a sick conspiracy, citing competition with China. China's government denies it is engaged in malicious competition over AI. Some Silicon Valley executives remain openly sceptical of the warnings.

Sport.

League. The Warriors' Adam Pompey has escaped a ban for the shoulder charge that saw him sin binned in Saturday's qualifying final loss to the Dolphins. He is free to play in this Sunday's sudden death elimination final against the Newcastle Knights at Eden Park, the last home game of their season. Warriors boss Cameron George has urged ticket scalpers to stay away from genuine fans.

Football. Erling Haaland's controversial winner stood as Manchester City beat Manchester United one nil in Saturday's derby, despite City playing more than seventy minutes with ten men after Phil Foden's red card. The video assistant referee for this weekend's derby, Matt Donohue, has not been appointed for this weekend's Premier League fixtures. Former West Ham and Czech Republic goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko has died aged sixty four.

Tennis. Alexander Zverev won the United States Open, beating Ben Shelton six three, six six, five seven, six two in the final. It is his second Grand Slam title.

Triathlon. New Zealander Hayden Wilde has won the Ironman seventy point three world half ironman title in France. It comes two years after he narrowly missed the title in Taupō.

Cricket. Michael Bracewell took five wickets for twelve runs, a career best T twenty haul, for Amsterdam against Edinburgh opponents who included two Black Caps teammates.

Rugby. Ardie Savea and Luke Jacobson will miss the Bledisloe Cup test. Scott Barrett is back in camp with Taranaki, working through return to play protocols.

Coming up. The Warriors play Newcastle at Eden Park this Sunday in an NRL elimination semifinal. NRL finals continue this week to decide the Grand Final field. The Bledisloe Cup test approaches, with Savea and Jacobson unavailable.

End of flash.
